title: LLM codegen fails and how to stop 'em — Danilo Campos, PostHog
talk_summary: Danilo Campos describes how PostHog's Wizard (an autonomous codegen agent doing ~15k integrations/month) fails and the mitigations: fresh markdown context to fight model rot, thin 'model airplane' reference projects, breadcrumbed step-by-step prompting instead of upfront specs, end-of-run self-interrogation to surface harness bugs, and locked-down tool permissions. The core thesis is that value lives in prose/skills and sequenced context, not in heavy scaffolding.

takeaways.what_they_do: At the stop hook of every run, ask the agent a simple question about what would have set it up for success, then mine the answers for harness bugs.
takeaways.evidence_quote: at the end of every run, uh right at the stop hook, we ask a very simple question... what could we have done better to set you up for success in this run
takeaways.numbers: found bugs that persisted across 'hundreds of runs' (missing tool, contradictory MCP directives, JS instructions on a Python project)

takeaways.technique: Breadcrumbed sequencing instead of upfront specs
takeaways.what_they_do: Don't tell the agent the full goal up front; issue small discovery-first steps (find business-relevant files, list candidate events, then implement) so it doesn't tunnel a 'Claude-code-shaped hole' through early tasks.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if you tell them exactly where you want to go, it might make a Claude code-shaped hole through the first four tasks and then just get really rock polishy with the fifth

takeaways.what_they_do: Maintain minimal simulacra of real apps (auth that accepts anything, etc.) flattened into a markdown skill file so the agent sees the correct shape of a successful integration and can grep it.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we maintain a fleet of what we call model airplanes... something that is a simulacrum of a real application... the off works for anything

takeaways.what_they_do: The Wizard is ~90% markdown skill files plus small tools to deliver/process markdown; they deliberately avoid over-constraining the agent with code scaffolds.
takeaways.evidence_quote: The wizard that makes everybody so happy is 90% markdown files, 8% tools for delivering and processing markdown files

takeaways.technique: Fine-grained tool permissions with purpose-built narrow tools
takeaways.what_they_do: Block agents from reading .env files directly; instead expose a tool that only checks key presence or writes a key value, so secrets never enter inference/logs.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we really locked down what the agent was allowed to do around anything that was an ENV file... It could check the presence of a key... and it could write to a key a new value

takeaways.technique: Fresh docs served on demand via tool selection
takeaways.what_they_do: Rather than static RAG, the agent detects what it's working on and uses tools to pull the matching fresh markdown doc into context.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we allow the agent to make a selection... pick from a menu of fresh hot markdown that it can then just slide right into its context
